mappings.note: Aqua regia dissolves gold. An acid acting on a metal, LO-3; the frame has no separate slot for aqua regia.

Citric acid is not a mineral acid. Sorting mineral from organic acids is a classification of substances with no learning outcome here -- LO-3 distinguishes acids from BASES -- so the C 1.2 competency is cited.
Ethanol is not a base. Deciding what counts as a base, LO-3.
Picks the false statement among carbonate-acid, oxide-water and metal-acid reactions. These are exactly the reactions LO-3 lists.
Matches bleaching powder, baking soda, borax and salt to their applications. Uses of LO-5's substances.
Equal volumes of equimolar HCl and NaOH give a neutral solution and green pH paper. The reaction is LO-3, but what is asked for is the pH-paper colour, which is LO-4.
HCl ionising in water to give hydronium ions. The H+ basis of acidity, LO-4.
Acids are sour and turn blue litmus red. Distinguishing acids from bases with an indicator, LO-3.
Which species are present in dilute HCl (H3O+ and Cl-). Ionisation and H+, LO-4.

Picks the correctly written chlor-alkali equation, states included. This is equation-writing but NOT a neutralisation or acid-on-metal reaction, so C 1.3-LO-3 does not fit and the competency is cited.
Matches lactic, acetic, citric and tartaric acids to curd, vinegar, lemon and tamarind. Natural sources of acids have no learning outcome in this frame; competency cited.
Matches plaster of Paris, gypsum and bleaching powder to their formulae. LO-5's substances.
Action of listed substances on blue litmus. The substances are not rendered by the tool, but the demand -- an indicator test separating acids from bases -- is fixed, LO-3.
Formic acid in an ant sting and relief by a mild base. An everyday-pH case, LO-4, as with the wasp-sting item.
Egg shell in nitric acid -- carbonate attacked, CO2 released. The acid-carbonate reaction of LO-3.

Tell an acid from a base with no litmus available. The content is LO-3; devising an alternative test is inquiry design, cited at C 8.2 rather than C 8.2-LO-1, which is about pH-testing household substances.
Distinguishing baking soda from washing soda by heating. Properties of both LO-5 substances.
Baking soda heated to washing soda plus CO2, identified by lime water. Preparation and properties of LO-5's substances.
Chlorine from NaOH manufacture reacting with lime water to give bleaching powder, with equations. Preparation of bleaching powder, LO-5.
Defines strong and weak acids and sorts six of them. Strength is the degree of ionisation, i.e. the H+ concentration behind LO-4.
Zinc with a dilute strong acid giving hydrogen, plus the pop test -- LO-3 -- and the balanced equation the question demands, C 1.3-LO-3.

Predicts the effect of changing one variable at a time in the hydrogen-preparation set-up (zinc dust, HCl for H2SO4, copper, NaOH). The chemistry is LO-3; changing a single variable and predicting is C 8.2.
Baking soda versus baking powder, the bitter taste, and the role of tartaric acid. Composition and use of baking soda, LO-5.
Ends at bleaching powder for disinfecting water, so LO-5; the opening step is a metal carbonate attacked by acid and the CO2 tested in lime water, which is LO-3.
Sodium hydroxide reacting with an acidic oxide -- a neutralisation in LO-3's 'with each other' sense -- and the balanced equation the question asks for, C 1.3-LO-3.
A Group 2 sulphate that can be moulded and then sets -- plaster of Paris, with the setting reaction. LO-5 names it.
Strong monobasic and weak dibasic acids with formulae. Strong versus weak is LO-4; basicity (mono/di) has no outcome in this frame and rides along.
Show experimentally that acetic acid is monobasic. The demonstration is a neutralisation against a base (LO-3), and devising and running it is C 8.2; monobasicity itself has no outcome.
Why NaOH and KOH must be kept stoppered -- they take up moisture and atmospheric CO2. A base reacting with an acidic oxide falls under LO-3's 'with each other'.
pH falling from 3 to 2 means a tenfold rise in H+. The pH scale, LO-4.
Washing soda crystals effloresce in air. A property of washing soda, LO-5.
Washing soda solution is alkaline. A property of washing soda, LO-5; the question names the substance rather than asking for a pH reading.
Chemical name and formula of baking soda. LO-5's substance.
Phenolphthalein turning pink shows the solution is basic. Indicator use, LO-3.
pH 2 is the stronger acid. The pH scale, LO-4.
Nature of sodium hydrogencarbonate -- mildly basic. The question asks for the acid/base character, so LO-4; LO-5 owns the substance but not this judgement.
Two salts of the chloride family. Grouping salts into families has no learning outcome in this frame -- LO-5 lists four specific salts and these are not them -- so the competency is cited.
Methyl orange's colour in a base. Indicator use, LO-3.
Gas from dilute HCl on sodium hydrogencarbonate, and the lime-water test. Acid on a carbonate, LO-3.
Orders NaOH, blood and lemon juice by pH. The pH scale applied to everyday substances, LO-4.
How dilution moves the pH of a base. The pH scale, LO-4.
Which solution holds more H+. The options are not printed, but the comparison itself is LO-4 whichever pair is intended.
Which bases count as alkalis, with an example. Defining bases, LO-3.
Natural sources of citric, oxalic, lactic and tartaric acid. Sources of acids have no outcome here; competency cited, as with 84979.
Main product of heating baking soda (sodium carbonate). Properties of baking soda, LO-5.
Gypsum heated at 373 K gives plaster of Paris and water. Preparation of plaster of Paris, LO-5.

A student pH-tests distilled water and then a common-salt solution and reads the paper. This is C 8.2-LO-1 almost literally -- testing the pH of a household substance -- with LO-4 supplying the neutral-pH reasoning.
Rain water at pH 6 versus pH 5. Comparing acidity on the pH scale, LO-4.
Alcohol solution does not conduct because it releases no ions. The H+ criterion of LO-4, the mirror of the HCl conductivity item.
The acid in a bee sting. An everyday-pH case, LO-4.
Calcium phosphate in tooth enamel. Part of LO-4's tooth-decay pH case.
A base reacting with a non-metallic oxide shows that oxide is acidic. An acid-base reaction, LO-3's 'with each other'.
Which acid and base give potassium sulphate and calcium chloride. Working a neutralisation backwards, LO-3; no balanced equation is demanded, so not C 1.3-LO-3.
pH of salts from strong-acid/strong-base and strong-acid/weak-base pairs. The pH of a salt solution, LO-4.
Two substances with water of crystallisation and their formulae -- washing soda and gypsum. Their formulae and properties are LO-5.
pH of distilled water and of salt solution, both 7. The neutral point of the pH scale, LO-4.
Which of pH 5 and pH 2 is the stronger acid. The pH scale, LO-4. (This duplicates 85004 -- see defect list.)
Orders pH 4, 9 and 6 by acidic strength. The pH scale, LO-4.
